title: Robots in Hospitals
summary: How robots help in hospitals by assisting surgeons, delivering supplies, killing germs, and connecting faraway doctors with patients, while people still make the decisions and give the care.
poll: One day, robots will do most of the work in hospitals.

versions.title: Robots That Help the Sick
versions.text:
Some robots work in a hospital. They help the sick get well. They do not get tired.

One kind helps fix the body. This doctor is a surgeon. The robot has long arms. Each arm holds a tool. The surgeon sits at a desk. She moves her hands. The arms move the same way. The robot does not choose. The surgeon is the boss!

The tools are small. So the cuts are small, too. Small cuts can heal fast.

A team in Riyadh used a robot. It helped give a teen a new heart. That was a first!

Some robots bring things. They roll down the halls. They take food to each room.

Some kill germs. Germs can make us sick. It shines a strong light in a room. The light kills the germs.

A doctor may be far off. A robot with a screen can help. You see her face on it. She can talk to the sick child.

Robots help a lot. But nurses still care for us. So do doctors. A robot can not smile at you!

versions.title: Robots That Help the Sick
versions.text:
Some robots work in a hospital. They help sick people get well. They do not get tired. They can work all day and all night.

One kind of robot helps a doctor do an operation. This doctor is a surgeon. The robot has long arms. Each arm holds a small tool. The surgeon sits at a desk near the bed. She moves her hands. Then the arms move the same way. The robot does not choose what to do. The surgeon is in charge!

The tools are very small. So the cuts in the skin can be small, too. Small cuts heal faster.

In Saudi Arabia, a team in Riyadh used a robot to help give a teen a new heart. It was the first time in the world!

Some robots carry things. They roll down the halls by themselves. They bring food, pills, and clean sheets to each room.

Some robots kill germs. Germs are tiny things that can make us sick. The robot shines a strong light in an empty room. The light kills the germs.

Sometimes a doctor is far away. A robot with a screen can help. The doctor's face shows on the screen. Then the doctor can talk with the sick child.

Robots are a big help. But nurses and doctors still care for us. A robot can not give a kind smile!

versions.title: Robots in the Hospital
versions.text:
When you think of a hospital, you may think of doctors and nurses. But in many hospitals, robots are part of the team, too. They help sick people get well. And they never get tired!

One kind of robot helps a doctor during an operation. A doctor who does operations is called a surgeon. The robot has long arms. Each arm holds a tiny tool or a small camera. The surgeon sits at a desk near the bed and looks at a screen. When she moves her hands, the robot arms move the same way. The robot does not decide what to do. The surgeon is always in charge.

The tools are very small. So the cuts in the skin can be small, too. Small cuts often hurt less and heal faster.

In 2024, doctors in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, used a robot to help give a teen a new heart. It was the first time this was done in the world!

Other robots carry things. They roll through the halls on their own. They bring meals, medicine, and clean sheets to each room.

Some robots fight germs. Germs are tiny living things that can make us sick. The robot shines a special light in an empty room. The light kills the germs.

Sometimes a doctor is far away. A robot with a screen can roll into the room. The doctor's face shows on the screen. Then the doctor can talk with the patient.

Robots are a big help. But nurses and doctors still give the care and kindness that sick people need.

versions.title: Robots in the Hospital
versions.text:
When you think of a hospital, you probably picture doctors and nurses rushing down the halls. But in many hospitals today, robots are part of the team as well. They help patients get better. And they never get tired.

One kind of robot helps during operations. A doctor who does operations is a surgeon. The robot has long arms. Each arm holds a tiny tool or a small camera. The surgeon sits at a desk a few steps away. She looks at a screen. When she moves her hands, the robot arms copy the same moves. The robot does not make choices. The surgeon controls every move.

Because the tools are so small, the cuts in the skin can be small, too. Small cuts usually hurt less and heal faster.

In 2024, doctors at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, used a robot to help give a teenage patient a new heart. It was the first time this was done in the world.

Other robots work as helpers. They move through the halls on their own. They carry meals, medicine, and supplies to the right rooms.

Some robots fight germs. These tiny living things spread sickness. The robot shines a special light around an empty room, and the light kills the germs.

Sometimes a doctor is far from the hospital. A robot with a screen can roll into a patient's room. The doctor's face shows on the screen, so the two can talk.

Robots are a big help. But nurses and doctors still give the care and kindness that patients need.

versions.title: Robots in Hospitals
versions.text:
Picture a busy hospital. Doctors and nurses hurry from room to room. Phones ring at the desk. But some of the workers here are not people at all. In many hospitals around the world, robots now help care for patients.

One important kind of robot helps surgeons. The robot has thin arms that hold tiny tools and a camera. The surgeon sits at a desk a few steps away. She looks into a viewer that shows a big, clear picture of the inside of the body. When she moves her hands, the robot arms copy each move in a smaller, very precise way. The robot never decides anything on its own. The surgeon controls every move.

Because the tools are so small, surgeons can make tiny cuts instead of large ones. Many patients feel less pain and go home sooner. In 2024, a team at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, used a robot to help give a teenage patient a new heart. It was the first time this was done in the world.

Other robots work behind the scenes. Some deliver meals, medicine, and supplies. They move through the halls on their own. They can even ride the elevators. Others help disinfect rooms. After a patient leaves, a robot shines a strong light around the empty room to kill germs.

Some robots let doctors work from far away. With a remote robot, a doctor in another city can appear on a screen. She can talk with a patient and help the team.

Robots save time and cut down on mistakes. Still, they cannot take the place of the people who listen, comfort, and make the big choices.

versions.title: Robots in Hospitals: Helpers, Not Replacements
versions.text:
Picture a busy hospital, where doctors and nurses hurry from room to room while telephones ring at the front desk. Yet some of the workers here are not people at all, because in many hospitals around the world, robots now help care for patients.

One important kind of robot assists surgeons during operations. The machine has several slender arms that hold miniature instruments and a camera. The surgeon sits at a console, a control station a few steps from the patient, and looks into a viewer that displays an enlarged, three-dimensional image of the inside of the body. When the surgeon moves her hands, the robotic arms reproduce each motion in a smaller, extremely precise way, and the system can even filter out a slight shake of the hand. However, the robot never makes decisions by itself. The surgeon controls every movement.

Because the instruments are so small, surgeons can work through a tiny incision, or cut, instead of a large opening, so many patients experience less pain and return home sooner. In 2024, a team at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, used a surgical robot to help give a teenage patient a new heart, the first operation of its kind in the world.

Other robots work behind the scenes. Delivery robots are autonomous, meaning they can move without a person steering them. With sensors and digital maps, they carry meals, medicine, and laboratory samples through the hallways and even ride the elevators. Disinfection robots enter empty rooms after patients leave and shine powerful ultraviolet light, which destroys many germs but is harmful to people.

In hospital pharmacies, robots sort and count thousands of pills each day. They read barcodes to check each medicine, which helps prevent mistakes that could harm patients.

Some robots support rehabilitation, the process of recovering strength and skills after an injury or illness. Wearable robotic frames, for example, can help a patient practice walking again. Remote robots with screens allow a specialist in another city to speak with a patient and guide the local medical team.

Robots save time and reduce errors. Nevertheless, they cannot replace the people who listen, comfort patients, and make the important decisions.

versions.title: Robots in Hospitals: Helpers, Not Replacements
versions.text:
Picture, for a moment, a bustling hospital in which physicians and nurses hurry briskly from room to room while telephones ring persistently at the reception desk. Yet not every worker contributing to patient care here is actually human, since in an increasing number of hospitals around the world, robots now participate meaningfully in the delivery of care.

One particularly significant category of robot assists surgeons directly during operative procedures. The machine itself possesses several slender mechanical arms, each holding miniature surgical instruments alongside a camera. The surgeon, seated at a console, a dedicated control station positioned only a short distance from the patient, peers into a viewer that displays a magnified, three-dimensional image of the body's interior anatomy. As the surgeon moves her hands, the robotic arms faithfully reproduce each motion in a smaller, extraordinarily precise manner, and the integrated system can even filter out a slight, involuntary tremor of the human hand; nevertheless, the robot never makes decisions independently, since the surgeon retains complete control over every movement throughout the procedure.

Because the instruments employed are so diminutive, surgeons can operate through a comparatively tiny incision rather than a large conventional opening, and consequently many patients experience markedly less postoperative discomfort and return home considerably sooner than they otherwise would. In 2024, a specialized team at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, employed a surgical robot to help provide a teenage patient with a new heart, the first operation of its particular kind performed anywhere in the world.

Other robots, meanwhile, operate largely behind the scenes, unseen by most patients. Delivery robots are genuinely autonomous, meaning they navigate hospital corridors without any human operator steering them directly; relying instead upon onboard sensors and detailed digital maps, they transport meals, medication, and laboratory specimens throughout the building and even operate elevators independently. Disinfection robots, by contrast, enter unoccupied rooms once patients have departed and emit powerful ultraviolet radiation, which destroys numerous microorganisms effectively but remains simultaneously hazardous to any human present in the room.

Within hospital pharmacies, additional robots sort and package thousands of individual medication doses daily, scanning barcodes meticulously to verify each medication and thereby helping to prevent errors that could otherwise seriously endanger patients.

Certain robots support rehabilitation, the demanding process of recovering strength and physical abilities following an injury or illness; wearable robotic exoskeletal frames, for instance, can help a recovering patient practice walking again with appropriate support. Remote robots equipped with video screens, meanwhile, enable a specialist physician located in an entirely different city to communicate directly with a patient and guide the local medical team, an arrangement particularly valuable for communities situated far from major medical centers.

Although robots unquestionably save considerable time and substantially reduce error rates throughout the hospital, they remain fundamentally incapable of replacing the compassionate human professionals who listen attentively, comfort anxious patients, and make the essential clinical decisions that machines alone cannot.

versions.title: Robots in Hospitals: Helpers, Not Replacements
versions.text:
Picture, for a moment, a bustling hospital in which physicians and nurses hurry briskly from room to room while telephones ring persistently and insistently at the reception desk. Yet not every individual contributing meaningfully to patient care within this environment is actually human, since in an increasing number of hospitals across the world, robots now participate substantively in the delivery of clinical care.

One particularly significant category of robot assists surgeons directly during delicate operative procedures. The machine itself possesses several slender mechanical arms, each equipped with miniature surgical instruments alongside an integrated camera. The surgeon, seated comfortably at a console, a dedicated control station positioned only a short distance from the operating table, peers intently into a viewer that displays a magnified, three-dimensional rendering of the patient's internal anatomy. As the surgeon moves her hands with practiced precision, the robotic arms faithfully reproduce each individual motion in a smaller, extraordinarily precise and scaled-down manner, and the integrated system can even computationally filter out a slight, involuntary tremor of the human hand; nevertheless, the robot never makes clinical decisions independently of human judgment, since the surgeon retains absolute control over every movement throughout the entirety of the procedure.

Because the surgical instruments employed are so diminutive in scale, surgeons can operate through a comparatively tiny incision rather than a large, traditionally invasive opening, and consequently many patients experience markedly less postoperative discomfort and are able to return home considerably sooner than they otherwise would under conventional surgical approaches. In 2024, a specialized surgical team at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, employed a surgical robot to help provide a teenage patient with a new heart, the first operation of its particular kind performed successfully anywhere in the world.

Other robots, meanwhile, operate largely behind the scenes, entirely unseen by most hospitalized patients. Delivery robots are genuinely autonomous, meaning they navigate hospital corridors independently without any human operator steering them directly in real time; relying instead upon an array of onboard sensors and continuously updated digital maps, they transport meals, medication, and laboratory specimens throughout the building and even operate elevators without human assistance. Disinfection robots, by contrast, enter unoccupied rooms once patients have been safely discharged or relocated, and emit powerful ultraviolet radiation, which destroys numerous pathogenic microorganisms with considerable efficiency but remains simultaneously hazardous to any human present within the room during exposure.

Within hospital pharmacies, additional specialized robots sort and package thousands of individual medication doses on a daily basis, methodically scanning barcodes to verify each specific medication and thereby helping to prevent potentially serious errors that could otherwise seriously endanger vulnerable patients.

Certain robots exist specifically to support rehabilitation, the demanding and often lengthy process of recovering strength and physical abilities following an injury or serious illness; wearable robotic exoskeletal frames, for instance, can help a recovering patient practice walking again with carefully calibrated mechanical support. Remote robots equipped with video screens, meanwhile, enable a specialist physician located in an entirely different city to communicate directly and in real time with a patient, guiding the local medical team through unfamiliar procedures, an arrangement particularly valuable for communities situated far from major medical centers and specialist expertise.

Although robots unquestionably save considerable time and substantially reduce error rates throughout virtually every department of the modern hospital, they remain fundamentally and permanently incapable of replacing the compassionate human professionals who listen attentively, comfort anxious patients and families, and make the essential, nuanced clinical decisions that machines alone cannot responsibly undertake.

keyWords.definition: tiny living things that can make people sick

By letting a doctor from another city speak with the patient
By riding the elevator to the roof
questions.why: A remote robot lets a faraway doctor appear on a screen, talk with the patient, and help the local team.

wrong.A: The robot does not carry patients.
wrong.B: Robots in the article never decide on their own.
wrong.D: Riding elevators is what delivery robots do.

questions.stem: The phrase "robots work behind the scenes" suggests that these robots
options: perform on a stage for patients
do helpful jobs that patients may not notice
work only at night when it is dark
are kept hidden because they are dangerous to patients
questions.why: Delivery and cleaning robots do quiet support jobs out of view, unlike the robots in operations.

wrong.A: Behind the scenes is an expression, not a real stage.
wrong.C: The article does not say they work only at night.
wrong.D: The article does not call them dangerous.

questions.stem: How is the article organized?
options: It tells the history of robots from oldest to newest.
It compares hospitals in two countries.
It describes a problem and then one solution.
It describes different kinds of hospital robots, one after another.
questions.why: The article moves from surgical robots to delivery, cleaning, and remote robots, then sums up.

wrong.A: There is no timeline of robot history.
wrong.B: The article does not compare countries.
wrong.C: Several kinds of robots are described, not one solution.

MID.prompt: The article says robots cannot replace the people who work in hospitals. Do you agree? Use two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I clearly said whether I agree.
I used two details from the article.
I explained how each detail supports my answer.
MID.modelAnswer: I agree that robots cannot replace the people who work in hospitals. For example, the surgery robot never decides anything on its own; the surgeon controls every move, which shows that human judgment is still needed. Also, even though delivery robots can disinfect rooms and deliver medicine, they cannot comfort a patient the way a nurse or doctor can. These details show that robots are helpful, but people are still essential in a hospital.

keyWords.definition: a control station with screens and handles used to operate a machine
keyWords.example: The pilot checked the lights on the console before takeoff.

keyWords.definition: a cut made on purpose, especially by a surgeon
keyWords.example: The vet made a small incision to remove the splinter.

keyWords.definition: able to act or move without someone controlling it
keyWords.example: The autonomous lawn mower cut the grass while we were at school.

keyWords.definition: describing invisible light from the Sun or lamps that can burn skin and kill germs
keyWords.example: Sunscreen protects your skin from ultraviolet rays.

keyWords.definition: the process of getting strength and skills back after an injury or illness
keyWords.example: After his knee injury, the player spent months in rehabilitation.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Robots now make the key medical decisions in hospitals.
Robots extend what hospital staff can do, but human judgment and compassion remain essential.
Robots are useful only for cleaning.
Robots are too expensive for most hospitals.
questions.why: The article describes surgical, delivery, disinfection, pharmacy, rehabilitation, and remote robots, then stresses that people still decide and comfort.

wrong.A: The surgeon controls every movement, and people make the decisions.
wrong.C: Cleaning is only one of many robot jobs.

questions.stem: What does the surgeon use the console for?
options: To scan barcodes on medicine
To steer delivery robots
To control the robotic arms while viewing a 3D image
To talk with a specialist who is working in another city
questions.why: The surgeon sits at the console, looks into a viewer, and moves her hands to guide the robotic arms.

wrong.B: Delivery robots are autonomous and need no one to steer them.
wrong.D: Remote robots with screens do that.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do disinfection robots work in empty rooms?
options: Ultraviolet light is harmful to people.
Germs only live in empty rooms.
The robots are too large to fit near beds.
Patients find the robots too noisy.
questions.why: The article says ultraviolet light destroys germs but is harmful to people, so rooms must be empty.

wrong.B: Germs are not limited to empty rooms.

questions.stem: The article calls delivery robots "autonomous." Which detail best shows this meaning?
options: They carry meals and samples.
They are found in many hospitals.
They have screens so faraway doctors can see and speak to patients.
They navigate using sensors and maps with no one steering.
questions.why: Moving without a person steering shows they act on their own, which is what autonomous means.

wrong.A: This tells what they carry, not how they move.
wrong.B: Being common does not show independence.

questions.stem: How is a surgical robot different from a delivery robot, according to the article?
options: The surgical robot moves on its own, but the delivery robot is steered.
The surgical robot copies a person's movements, while the delivery robot moves on its own.
Both robots need a surgeon to work.
Both robots shine ultraviolet light.
questions.why: The surgeon controls every movement of the surgical robot, while delivery robots are autonomous.

wrong.C: Delivery robots do not need a surgeon.
wrong.D: Only disinfection robots use ultraviolet light.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the 2024 operation in Riyadh?
options: To prove robots can operate without surgeons
To compare Saudi hospitals with hospitals in other countries
To show how robot-assisted surgery is reaching new milestones
To describe how hearts work
questions.why: A first-of-its-kind heart operation shows how far robot-assisted surgery has come.

wrong.A: A surgical team used the robot; it did not act alone.
wrong.B: No comparison between countries is made.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why the robot filters out a slight tremor of the surgeon's hand?
options: Tiny unwanted movements could cause harm inside the body.
Surgeons often have weak hands.
The robot wants to make its own decisions.
The console cannot read the surgeon's normal, steady hand movements.
questions.why: Because the work is extremely precise, even a small shake could damage tissue, so removing it adds safety.

wrong.B: The article does not say surgeons have weak hands.

questions.stem: Which group would most likely benefit from remote robots, based on the article?
options: Surgeons who want bigger incisions
Patients far from specialists
Pharmacists who count pills
Robots that need repairs
questions.why: Remote robots let a specialist in another city speak with a patient and guide the local team, which helps people far from specialists.

wrong.A: Robots help make smaller incisions, not bigger ones.
wrong.C: Pharmacy robots, not remote robots, help count pills.

HIGH.prompt: Imagine your local hospital can buy only one kind of robot from the article. Which should it choose? Support your choice with evidence and explain one thing the robot still cannot do without people.
checklist: I chose one robot and stated my choice clearly.
I supported it with specific evidence from the article.
I explained a limit that shows people are still needed.
HIGH.modelAnswer: If my local hospital could buy only one kind of robot, I would choose the surgical robot. The evidence from the article shows that a team in Riyadh used this kind of robot to perform the first operation of its kind in the world, giving a teenage patient a new heart, and its tiny incisions help patients feel less pain and recover sooner. However, this robot still cannot do everything without people, because it is not autonomous: the surgeon sitting at the console must control every movement, since the robot never decides anything on its own.
